explanations.answer: God does not allow him to enjoy them
explanations.explanation: That's the evil the Teacher spotted. The man has riches, wealth and honor, and the text says God does not allow him to enjoy them. Nothing is missing from his pile except the enjoying. I think that's why the Teacher calls it a weight on mankind (Ecclesiastes 6:1).

explanations.answer: He loses all of it in one night
explanations.explanation: Close to a sad story, but it's not the one the Teacher tells. Nobody here loses everything overnight. The man lacks nothing his heart desires, and the trouble is that God does not allow him to enjoy what he has. The riches are sitting right there.

explanations.answer: His honor slowly turns into shame
explanations.explanation: The text never says his honor turns into anything. He has riches, wealth and honor, and he lacks nothing his heart desires. What the Teacher points to is that God does not allow him to enjoy them, and a stranger will enjoy them instead. Shame never walks into this verse.

Yes, baker. The Teacher says a stranger will enjoy what the man couldn't, and then he says, "This is futile and a grievous affliction." Those are his own words for it. He doesn't tiptoe around how heavy it is.

The text says the opposite. After saying a stranger will enjoy the man's riches, the Teacher says, "This is futile and a grievous affliction." He doesn't shrug it off or call it fine. He names it as a real hardship, plain and direct.

It sounds like it should, doesn't it? A hundred children and many years feel like they'd cover a lot. But the Teacher says the opposite. If the man is unsatisfied with his prosperity and does not even receive a proper burial, no matter how long he lives, he says a stillborn child is better off than he. All those years don't cancel that out.

That's right. A hundred children and many years sound like a full life, but the Teacher says no matter how long he lives, if the man is unsatisfied with his prosperity and does not even receive a proper burial, a stillborn child is better off than he. So the long life and the big family don't make up for it. I think this is a hard line, and it's worth sitting with.

That's the comparison the Teacher makes, and I think this is a heavy one. He says he's talking about a man who is unsatisfied with his prosperity and doesn't even receive a proper burial. Next to that man, he says a stillborn child is better off. He's showing how deep the emptiness runs for a man who never enjoys what he has.

No widow appears in these verses. The Teacher is describing a man with a hundred children and many years who is unsatisfied with his prosperity. The one he says is better off than that man is a stillborn child. I think it's a heavy line, and he chose it on purpose.

A foreigner never comes up here. The only person set beside the unsatisfied man is a stillborn child. The Teacher says that child is better off than he. I think it's a hard thing to read, and it's okay to feel that.

Rest is the word. The Teacher says the child, though neither seeing the sun nor knowing anything, has more rest than that man. It's a heavy thing to say, and I think he's showing how restless a life of unenjoyed riches can be. The man has everything and can't settle into any of it.

Joy isn't the word the Teacher uses. He says the child neither sees the sun nor knows anything, so joy isn't what he's measuring. What he says the child has more of is rest. It's a quiet word for a heavy comparison.

Hope never shows up in these verses. The Teacher says the child, though neither seeing the sun nor knowing anything, has more rest than the unsatisfied man. Rest is the thing being compared. I think it's a stark picture of how worn out that man is.

True. After all that, the Teacher asks, "Do not all go to the same place?" He asks it as a question and lets it hang there. I think he's reminding us that the length of a life doesn't change where it ends up.

The Teacher does ask it. Right after the thousand years twice over, he says, "Do not all go to the same place?" It's a question, and he leaves it open for us to chew on. So the comparison ends with that question hanging in the air.

That's what he says. All a man's labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied. It's like pressing a whole batch of cookies, eating one warm, and still reaching for the next. The work goes in and the wanting is still there.

The Teacher doesn't say anything about age shrinking an appetite. He says the man's labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied. Never is a long time, baker. The work goes in and the wanting stays right where it was.

explanations.answer: It is filled by hard work
explanations.explanation: You'd think so, since all that labor is for the mouth. But the Teacher says the man's appetite is never satisfied. So the hard work doesn't fill it. It keeps going while the appetite stays hungry.

explanations.answer: What advantage he has over the fool
explanations.explanation: Right. The Teacher asks, "What advantage, then, has the wise man over the fool?" He doesn't answer it in these verses. He just lets the question sit there. I think it's a question worth stopping to think about.

explanations.answer: Why he keeps his wisdom hidden
explanations.explanation: Nobody hides anything in these verses. The Teacher asks about the wise man, "What advantage, then, has the wise man over the fool?" It's a question about what wisdom gains him. Hiding it never comes up.

explanations.answer: Whether his name will last forever
explanations.explanation: A lasting name isn't the question here. The Teacher asks what advantage the wise man has over the fool. He's asking about the gain, not about being remembered. Names do come up a few verses later, but that's a different thought.

Flip that one around, baker. The Teacher says, "Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire." So the thing in front of you wins over the thing your mind keeps drifting toward. Then he adds that this too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.

That's it. The text says, "Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire." What's in front of you beats the wanting that wanders off. And the Teacher still says this too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
True. The Teacher says it's known what man is, but he cannot contend with one stronger than he. That's a plain fact about being human. I'd say it's a humbling one, and I've had my share of those.

The text says it right there. After saying it is known what man is, the Teacher says he cannot contend with one stronger than he. There's no twist hiding in it. It's a straight statement about where man stands.

That's his question. He says, "For the more words, the more futility—and how does that profit anyone?" He's asking what all those words actually gain. Looks like a lot of talkers just got a little quiet.

Listening isn't what he asks about. He says the more words, the more futility, and then asks how that profits anyone. His question is about the gain from the words. It's not about whether anybody hears them.
The fool isn't mentioned in this verse. The Teacher says the more words, the more futility, and then he asks how that profits anyone. It's about words in general. Nobody gets singled out.

It's the other way around, baker. The Teacher doesn't claim he can tell a man what's coming. He asks, "Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?" It's a question, and the whole verse is about how little we can know.

Yes, that's right. The Teacher asks, "Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?" He asks it as a question, not a claim. Just before that, he asks who knows what is good for a man in his few days.
